title: On Reactions To That Nikole Hannah-Jones Piece
author: Peter Greene
summary: Peter Greene offers five observations on the flood of reactions to Nikole Hannah-Jones's essay. He notes that the dilemma she describes has been faced countless times by less famous parents, and that he would never expect a parent to do anything but what they think best for their child. He objects to national debates centered on New York City, a system too large and idiosyncratic to be an example of anything but itself. Greene laments that instead of opening a discussion of segregation and unequal resources, the piece has prompted everyone to repeat their usual arguments, including the claim that exit will spur failing schools to improve. He highlights what the essay shows about engaged teachers and how choice sorts students by ability, and urges readers to go back to the essay's closing passage on collective apathy and the absence of absolution.
points: Greene sees the essay's dilemma as an old one faced by many ordinary parents without national attention.
New York City's school system, larger than Wyoming's population, is in his view not a model for other districts.
He argues the threat of exit already existed for Najya's school and did not spur improvement through market forces.
School choice, he notes, can segregate students by ability as well as by class.
Most responses, he says, amount to variations of I told you so rather than new thinking.
quotes: It has been an issue as long as we have had schools-- if you have the privileged ability to get your child away from a less-than-optimal school situation, do you use it, or are you betraying the people who don't have your privilege?
But while I have definite ideas about the policy issues involved in school choice, I would never expect a parent to do anything other than what they think is best for their child.

I get tired of discussion centered on the New York City school system, a system that by virtue of its size and complexity and politics (there are about 300,000 more students in the NYC school system than there are human beings in the state of Wyoming) is not an example of anything but itself.

It would be lovely if NHJ's piece opened up a meaningful discussion about those issues but, predictably, it has not. Instead, everyone is saying what they always say, yelling "Aha!" and rushing to make their usual arguments.
Mostly (mostly) just a hundred variations of "I told you so and now I will tell you so again.

NHJ's story underscores the importance of engaged and caring teachers, supportive staff, and parents who are willing to engage and push the school. And it also shows the ways that school choice segregate students not only by class, but by ability.
